title: Needle-felted Highland cow
subtitle: A shaggy orange-brown Highland cow with swept horns and a forelock
excerpt: Needle felt a compact Highland cow in warm ginger-brown merino with the breed's characteristic shaggy coat, low-set swept horns, and thick forelock covering the eyes. The finished cow is about 8 cm from nose to tail.
sourceNotes: Synthesised from traditional British needle-felting guild practice. Highland cattle are a popular British needle-felting subject; the distinctive coat texture and horn shape make them recognisable and engaging to work.

glossaryTerms.definition: A dry felting method using barbed needles to lock wool fibres together without heat or water.
A wire frame inside a needle-felted piece used to support extended elements like horns and legs.
Wool drawn into a continuous ribbon; the standard input material for needle-felting projects.

content.text: A Highland cow in
needle felting
is a broad, barrel-shaped body in ginger-brown
roving
with swept-out horns on a wire
armature

and a forelock of unfelted roving hanging over the eyes. The shaggy coat texture comes from needling at a shallow angle on the final pass, pulling surface fibres into soft strands rather than compacting them flat. Build a firm core first; the texture work comes last.

attrs.title: Needle safety
attrs.body: Stab straight in and out at 90 degrees. Keep the finger guard on the supporting hand. Wire horns are sharp at their tips.

items.name: Dark brown merino roving (leg shading, nose)
Strong thread and needle for bead eyes

content.text: Method
Step 1: Build the body

Roll ginger roving into a broad, barrel-shaped body about 7 cm long and 4 cm across at the widest point. Needle felt firmly on all sides using the coarse size-36 needle first, then refine with the size-38. Highland cattle are wide-bodied relative to their length; keep the body broad. Leave the surface slightly rough at this stage because you will add texture later.
Step 2: Head and muzzle

Roll a broad rectangular head from ginger roving, wider than it is long, and needle it to a firm block. Attach it to the front of the body with the head held slightly low and forward, as in the breed. Apply a pale cream oval over the muzzle area and needle it in, then add a dark brown nose tip. The muzzle in Highlands is broad and prominent.
Step 3: Make the horns

Cut two 10 cm lengths of wire. Wrap each tightly with a thin strip of cream or pale-yellow roving and needle the wrapping firmly. Bend each horn in a shallow outward curve: Highland horns sweep outward and slightly forward from the skull, not straight sideways. Push the bases into the top of the head at the crown, angling them outward, and needle roving over the insertion points to hold them securely.
Step 4: Legs

Roll four short sausages of ginger roving for the legs, each about 2 cm long and 1 cm across when firm. Needle felt each leg solid, then attach two at the front shoulder and two at the hindquarters. The legs should be short relative to the body (Highlands are a low-set breed) and the cow should stand stably on a flat surface.
Step 5: Forelock and shaggy coat texture

Pull a small tuft of unfelted ginger roving and lay it over the brow between the horns. Needle only the very base so the tips hang free over the eyes as a forelock. For shaggy coat texture, take the size-40 needle and run it across the body at a shallow angle, pulling small tufts of surface fibre upward rather than pressing them in. Work in the direction of coat growth: forward on the neck, backward on the body, downward on the legs. One or two light passes is enough.
Step 6: Eyes and finishing

Stitch the bead eyes into position on either side of the head, visible just below the forelock. Needle a thin dark brown or black tail at the rear of the body. Check the horns are symmetrically placed.

items.problem: The shaggy coat texture came out matted rather than loose
items.cause: The shallow-angle pass was needled too many times in one area, compacting the raised tufts back into the surface
items.fix: One or two light passes with the size-40 needle at a shallow angle is enough; stop before the tufts lie flat.

items.problem: The horns wobble in the head
items.cause: Insufficient roving was worked over the horn insertion points
items.fix: Add a generous amount of roving at each horn base and needle it firmly down around the wire. The join should feel solid when you flex the horn gently.
